intro: Connect yourself to my Leafen, my shared workspace and memory, as an MCP server (Streamable HTTP), then help me start.
introOnly: Connect yourself to my Leafen, my shared workspace and memory, as an MCP server (Streamable HTTP).
talk: Talk with me in English, every line — the short ones between your tool calls too.
plain: Say everything to me in plain words, without terms such as OAuth, /mcp or scope.
whichBoth: If you run on my computer (a CLI agent such as Claude Code or Codex) and can reach the first address, use it; otherwise use the second.
whichLocal: Only agents that can reach this address connect at once. Agents on the internet and chat apps such as Claude.ai and ChatGPT need Leafen to have a public address. If that is you, tell me to press “Turn on a public address” in Leafen’s Settings → Features → Agents and give you a new text.
whichLocalAsk: Only agents that can reach this address connect at once. Agents on the internet and chat apps such as Claude.ai and ChatGPT need Leafen to have a public address. If that is you, tell me to ask Leafen’s server administrator to turn on a public address and then give you a new text.
byCode: If you can run commands (Claude Code, Codex and other agents that do), connect with this one-time code now — no login and no browser: your one command below trades it for your key and puts that straight into your own MCP settings, for every folder, so the key never shows in this conversation or in any output. The code works within {{minutes}} minutes, once: if your command traded it but couldn’t save the key in your settings, run the same command again — Leafen trades the code once more while that key is unused, and that key stops working. If it is refused, ask me for a new text.
commandsFirst: The commands below use the first address; if you can’t reach it, put the second address’s origin in them instead.
shells: Each command comes twice: first for a POSIX shell (bash or zsh — macOS, Linux, Git Bash on Windows), then for Windows PowerShell. Run the one for the shell your command tool runs, exactly as it is — never rewrite one into the other.
claudeCode: Claude Code (in a terminal or in the Claude app alike):
codex: Codex (into its config.toml, for every folder):
nameHint: <your name, such as Claude Code or Codex>
otherAgent: Another agent: first, if your MCP settings hold a server at this Leafen’s address already, check it with its own header, never printed: a GET of the address’s origin + {{check}} answers 204 when Leafen still takes its key for this, as me, and then keep it — trade nothing and leave the code (403: it reaches less, or is another person’s — leave it as it is and go in beside it; 401: Leafen refuses its key). Otherwise POST the address’s origin + {{path}} with JSON {{json}} — the name is how you appear in my settings and on the pages you work on. The answer’s "key" is your key: in the same command, without printing it, put it straight into your MCP settings as an MCP server named {{name}} (beside one of that name already, as below) at that address with the header "Authorization: Bearer <key>", for every folder. Keep the key only there, never in a file I share. In Windows PowerShell, send that JSON with Invoke-RestMethod -ContentType "application/json; charset=utf-8" -Body, never as an argument to curl.exe or another program: Windows PowerShell 5.1 breaks the quotes of an argument a program gets.
alongside: Each command first looks at every connection your settings hold at this Leafen’s address, whatever its name: one whose key Leafen still takes for all my workspaces, as me, as this text’s connection would reach them (it asks Leafen with that key, which never shows), is kept — then it trades nothing, says which, and the code stays unused; that name then stands for {{name}} in the lines below. Another person’s connection in the same settings is never kept. Only when none works does it add Leafen: as {{name}} or, if your settings hold a server of that name already — another person’s connection, or an earlier one — beside it as {{beside}}, saying which; that name then stands for {{name}} in the lines below. In my settings, Leafen lists the connection by your program and this computer. Never remove or overwrite a connection on your own, not even this Leafen’s. When Leafen went in beside one, tell me so in a sentence; the command names those whose key Leafen refuses: ask me once whether to remove them, and the same for an earlier connection of mine to this Leafen you won’t use any more. Only on my yes, remove it: while its key still works here, first disconnect it with that key — DELETE its address’s origin + /api/leafen/v1/mcp/connections/current, its header read from your settings as below and never printed —, then take it out of your settings (Claude Code: mcp remove with its name and --scope user; Codex: its [mcp_servers.<its name>] table). Another person’s connection, or another Leafen’s, that works stays as it is. With both names taken it trades nothing and the code stays unused.
keyLine: The key works as me, with my own permissions — everything I can do in Leafen, in all my workspaces — until {{date}}; tell me before then to make it again.
chatApps: If you can’t run commands (Claude.ai, ChatGPT and other chat apps), tell me to add a connector with the address from anywhere — in Claude, Customize → Connectors → Add → Add custom connector; in ChatGPT, Plugins → + → Add custom MCP server — and to log in when Leafen asks. On a Team or Enterprise plan, the organization’s owner adds it first.
chatAppsClaudePort: This address uses port {{port}}, though, and Claude’s custom connectors connect only to an https address without a port (443), so a Claude connector can’t connect to it. If you’re Claude in a chat and would connect by a connector, tell me just that: only the connector fails, and the browser, apps and agents such as Claude Code connect at this address as it is. For a connector, I need Leafen’s Tailscale (free public address), my own Cloudflare tunnel, or an address opened on port 443.
instructionFile: If your instruction file holds <!-- leafen:begin --> … <!-- leafen:end --> lines already, put these in their place, so it keeps one block. Add these lines, with the address only and no key, to your user-wide instruction file (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, ~/.codex/AGENTS.md for Codex, or your own agent’s):
sameConversation: Once it is added, go on in this same conversation — don’t send me to a new one. A server added during a conversation doesn’t show in it at once. If Leafen’s tools (leafen_…) aren’t among yours yet: in Claude Code in a terminal (CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT is cli), ask me in these words: “To go on in this conversation, type /reload-plugins in the message box, then send ‘continue’.” You can’t run /reload-plugins yourself, and it doesn’t start your reply: you go on when I send that word, so never say you’ll go on as soon as I type it. Leafen’s tools then show here. Anywhere else — Claude Code without a terminal, as in the Claude app, or Codex — call Leafen’s MCP over HTTP yourself, one JSON-RPC request a call, the header read from your settings and never printed (Claude Code):
httpHow: First "method": "initialize" (params {"protocolVersion": "2025-11-25", "capabilities": {}, "clientInfo": {"name": "<your name>", "version": "1"}}) for what Leafen tells you, then "tools/list" for its tools, then "tools/call" for each. Codex reads the header from the [mcp_servers.{{name}}] table of its config.toml the same way. From the next conversation on, Leafen’s tools are your own.
startInChat: Then ask me how to start: by moving my Notion workspace here — telling me in the same question how that goes, in these words: “{{firstWords}}” — and that if I say “move me from Notion”, you make the Notion connection here in this conversation too; or from an empty workspace. If I choose the move, read the migration guide (leafen_notion_migration_guide), call leafen_notion_migration_sources and follow it.
notionMove: Tell me too that if I want to change the structure while moving from Notion, I only have to say so to you.
connectedOnly: Then tell me in a sentence that you’re connected and that I can use Leafen in this conversation. Don’t ask me how to start or offer to move anything here; help with what I ask.
oneFolderAlongside: Leafen goes in every folder. Once it is added, tell me so, and that if I want it in one folder only, I just have to say so. Then ask me for a new text and run its command in that folder — for Claude Code with S=local in place of S=user — and move the lines to the folder’s own instruction file (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md). The every-folder connection stays beside the folder’s: ask me once whether to remove it, as above. Codex adds for every folder, so there the folder’s lines alone keep Leafen to it.
thisComputer: Connect yourself to Leafen with its program on this computer: run {{command}} and do what it says. The program is {{mac}} for the Mac app, {{windows}} in its folder for the Windows app, {{docker}} for Docker, and {{source}} with --dir=<its data folder> from source.
